activities.title: The Magnet Timeline on a String

materials.item: a piece of string about 3 metres long
12 small cards or pieces of paper, and crayons
clothes pegs or tape

activities.safety: Tie the string low, below a child's shoulder, so nobody walks into it.

schedule.what: Make 12 history cards and hang them on a string in order.

activities.record: Take a photo of the finished timeline, or draw it.

flow.do: Help your child write and draw one card for each event: about 600 BCE Thales and the lodestone in Greece. About 240 BCE the Chinese 'loving stone'. The Sushruta Samhita's magnet for arrowheads in India. 1044 the Chinese south-pointing iron fish. 1088 Shen Kuo's needle. About 1232 al-Awfi in Delhi describes the floating fish. 1269 Peregrinus and the two poles. 1600 Gilbert says the Earth is a magnet. 1820 Oersted's compass moves near a wire. 1894 Marie Curie begins studying magnets in steel. 1936 Inge Lehmann finds the solid core. 1975 magnetic bacteria described.
flow.say: Let's make a timeline of how people learned about magnets. One card for each discovery, with a little drawing.
flow.kid: Make 12 cards. Each one is a magnet discovery. Write the year and draw a little picture.
flow.parent: The Sushruta Samhita is hard to date exactly. It was written down over many centuries, and the version we have is more than 1,500 years old. Put it between 240 BCE and 1044 with a question mark. BCE years count backwards: 600 BCE is earlier than 240 BCE.
flow.context: This is the first step of the magnet timeline. You make cards for discoveries about magnets, from ancient Greece, China and India to today.

flow.do: 1. Tie the string across a room, low down. 2. Peg the cards on in order, oldest on the left.
flow.say: Which is oldest? Which is newest? Let's put them in order.
flow.kid: Hang the cards on the string. Oldest on the left. Newest on the right.

options: William Gilbert saying the Earth is a magnet, in 1600
Shen Kuo describing a magnet needle, in 1088
Marie Curie studying magnets in steel, in 1894
check.why: 1088 is the smallest of the three years, so Shen Kuo came first. Gilbert came 512 years later, in 1600, and Marie Curie in 1894. Picking Gilbert is common, because many Western books start the story of magnets with him. The Chinese, Indian and Islamic stories come earlier.

flow.do: Stand back and look at the whole timeline together.
flow.say: Look at the places on our cards. Greece, China, India, France, England, Denmark and the USA. What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Look at all the places on your cards. Did one country find out everything?
flow.think: Two women are on our timeline. Can you find out about other women who studied magnets?

activities.context: In this activity you hang a timeline of magnet discoveries across a room. It shows how people in many countries added to what we know.

activities.title: Gilbert's Little Earth: a needle on a thread

materials.item: the magnetised needle from the floating compass experiment, or a newly stroked one
a piece of sewing thread about 30 cm long
a bar magnet or round magnet
a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up ties the thread to the needle.

schedule.what: Hang a magnetised needle on a thread. Walk it around a magnet and draw where it points.

activities.record: Draw the magnet in the middle of the paper, and an arrow at each place for where the needle pointed.

flow.do: 1. Tie the thread around the middle of the needle. 2. Slide the knot until the needle hangs level. 3. Hold the thread up, far from any iron. Watch the needle settle.
flow.say: This hanging needle is a compass. Watch it settle north and south.
flow.kid: Hang the needle on its thread. Keep it far from iron. Wait. Which way does it settle?
flow.context: This is the first step of Gilbert's Little Earth. In 1600, William Gilbert moved a tiny compass around a magnet ball. Here you do the same with a needle on a thread.

flow.do: 1. Put the magnet in the middle of the paper. 2. Hold the hanging needle about a hand's width from the magnet, at 8 places around it, like the numbers on a clock. 3. At each place, wait for it to settle and draw an arrow the way it points.
flow.say: Move the needle around the magnet slowly. Each time, draw which way it points.
flow.kid: Hold the needle near the magnet. Move it around, like the hands of a clock. At each place, draw an arrow for where it points.
flow.parent: Closer than a hand's width, the needle may jump onto the magnet. Further away, it starts to point north again, because there the Earth's magnetic field is stronger than the magnet's. Your arrows should curve around the magnet, from one end to the other, like the black sand lines.

flow.do: Compare the drawing to a picture of the Earth with a compass on it.
flow.say: Gilbert saw this and thought: a compass on the Earth behaves just like this. So the Earth must be a magnet.
flow.kid: Your needle pointed along curved lines around the magnet. A compass on the Earth does the same. What did Gilbert decide?

check.q: William Gilbert's tiny compass behaved the same around his magnet ball as compasses do on the real Earth. What did he decide?
options: The Earth is a giant magnet
Compasses are attracted to the Pole Star
Magnets only work on small balls
check.why: If a compass acts the same around a magnet ball as it does on the Earth, the simplest explanation is that the Earth is a magnet too. Before Gilbert, many people thought compasses were attracted by the Pole Star, or by a magnetic mountain in the far north. Picking the Pole Star means following that old idea.

activities.context: In this activity you copy William Gilbert's famous 1600 experiment. You move a hanging needle compass around a magnet and draw how it points.

activities.title: Find Your Beach: be a sea turtle

materials.item: a blindfold or a soft cloth
4 cards marked WEAK, MEDIUM, STRONG, VERY STRONG, and a cushion for the beach

activities.safety: Play in a clear room or on grass. A grown-up walks beside the blindfolded child.

schedule.what: Act out a young turtle finding their way home by sensing the strength of the Earth's magnetic field.

activities.record: Draw the path the turtle took.

flow.do: 1. Put a cushion at one end of the room. This is the beach. 2. Lay the 4 cards on the floor in a line leading to it. Put WEAK furthest away and VERY STRONG next to the beach.
flow.say: A young sea turtle has no map. But the Earth's magnetic field is a little different in every part of the ocean. Its strength changes, and so does the angle at which it dips into the Earth. Turtles can sense both.
flow.kid: The cushion is your home beach. Each card says how strong the Earth's magnetic field is there. You are a baby turtle. Can you find home?
flow.context: This is the first step of Find Your Beach. You act out how young sea turtles may find their way using the Earth's magnetic field.

flow.do: 1. Blindfold your child at the far end. 2. Walk beside them. Each time they step near a card, whisper what it says. 3. Let them choose which way to go by whether it gets stronger or weaker.
flow.say: Weak. Medium. Getting stronger. Which way is home?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Listen to how strong the field is. Stronger means you are getting closer. Find your beach!
flow.parent: This is a simple model. Real turtles seem to sense both the strength of the Earth's magnetic field and the angle at which it dips into the Earth. Together these work like a map. Kenneth and Catherine Lohmann showed this with loggerhead turtles. Each beach has its own magnetic 'address'.

flow.do: Take off the blindfold and talk.
flow.say: Olive ridley turtles nest on beaches in Odisha, at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya. They come back after years at sea. Scientists think they may find their beaches using the Earth's magnetic field.
flow.kid: You found home without seeing! Real olive ridley turtles cross the sea to Odisha's beaches. How do you think it feels to know the way?

check.q: How do scientists think young sea turtles find their way across the ocean?
options: They follow the boats
They sense the strength and the angle of the Earth's magnetic field
They remember the shapes of the waves
check.why: Experiments show that young turtles change direction when scientists change the magnetic field around them in a tank. Each part of the ocean has its own strength and angle of the Earth's magnetic field, like an address. Picking 'follow the boats' cannot be right. Turtles were crossing oceans for millions of years before there were boats.

activities.context: In this activity you act out a young sea turtle finding their way home across the ocean, by sensing the strength of the Earth's magnetic field.

activities.title: Paint an Aurora

materials.item: a sheet of black or dark blue paper
chalk, oil pastels or crayons in green, red, purple and white
a picture of the Earth's magnetic field, from the explanation cards

schedule.what: Paint auroras over mountains and add the Earth's magnetic field lines in a corner.

activities.record: Write one sentence under your picture about what makes auroras.

flow.do: Look together at a photo of an aurora, and the picture of the Earth's magnetic field.
flow.say: The Sun blows out tiny charged particles. The Earth's magnetic field steers them towards the poles. They hit the air high up and make it glow.
flow.kid: Look at the aurora. Tiny particles from the Sun hit the air. The Earth's magnetic field steers them to the poles. The air glows.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paint an Aurora. You learn what makes the lights near the poles, then paint them.

flow.do: 1. Draw dark mountains along the bottom. 2. Use the side of the chalk to sweep green curtains of light across the sky. 3. Add a little red at the top. 4. In one corner, draw the small Earth with its curved magnetic field lines.
flow.say: Sweep the chalk sideways, like a curtain blowing. Green is oxygen glowing lower down. Red is oxygen glowing higher up.
flow.kid: Draw mountains. Sweep green chalk across the sky like a curtain. Add red on top. Draw a little Earth with its field lines.

flow.do: Write a sentence under the picture.
flow.say: What makes the aurora? Say it in one sentence.
flow.kid: Write one sentence. What makes an aurora?

check.q: Why are auroras seen mostly near the North and South Poles?
options: Because it is cold there
Because the Earth's magnetic field steers the Sun's tiny charged particles towards the poles
Because there is ice to reflect the light
check.why: The Earth's magnetic field lines dip down into the Earth near the poles. The Sun's charged particles are steered along those lines, so most of them reach the air near the poles. Picking 'cold' or 'ice' links auroras with what the poles look like, not with what causes them. In May 2024, a big solar storm made auroras visible as far south as Ladakh.

activities.title: Heat Takes the Magnet Away

materials.item: a magnetised needle, from the floating compass experiment
kitchen tongs or pliers
a gas stove
a steel pin or a staple
a steel plate or tile to cool the needle on

activities.safety: Only a grown-up does the heating. Hold the needle with tongs or pliers, never fingers. The needle stays hot for a minute after it stops glowing. No gas stove? Watch the grown-up do it on a friend's stove, or skip to the last step.

schedule.what: A grown-up heats a magnetised needle until it glows. After it cools, test it on a pin. Then stroke it again.

activities.record: Write yes or no: picks up a pin before heating, after heating, and after stroking again.

flow.do: Test the magnetised needle on a pin first.
flow.say: First, let's check it's still a magnet.
flow.kid: Touch the needle to the pin. Is it still a magnet?
flow.context: This is the first step of Heat Takes the Magnet Away. A grown-up heats a magnetised needle to show that heat shakes its tiny magnets out of line.

flow.do: 1. Hold the needle by one end with tongs. 2. Put the other half in the hottest part of the gas flame, near the tip of the blue part. 3. Keep it there until it glows orange-red, about 30 seconds. 4. Lay it on the steel plate to cool for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Watch it glow. Heat makes the atoms jiggle. Will the tiny magnets stay lined up?
flow.kid: Stand back and watch the grown-up. The needle glows red! Heat makes its atoms jiggle hard. Wait 2 minutes for it to cool.
flow.parent: Iron loses its magnetism at about 770 degrees Celsius, when it glows dull red. A thin needle reaches this in a gas flame within a minute. Only the part that glowed loses its magnetism. So test the heated end against the pin.

flow.do: 1. When the needle is cool, touch its heated end to the pin. 2. Then stroke it 50 times with the magnet and test again.
flow.say: Is it still a magnet? And can we make it one again?
flow.kid: Touch the heated end to the pin. Does it stick? Now stroke it 50 times. Test again.

check.q: After heating until it glowed, the needle's end would not pick up the pin. Why?
options: The heat burned away the iron
The heat shook the tiny magnets out of line
The needle is now made of a different metal
check.why: Heat makes atoms jiggle. At about 770 degrees Celsius, iron's atoms jiggle so hard that the tiny magnets cannot stay lined up. The iron is still iron, which is why stroking can make it a magnet again. Picking 'burned away the iron' is a natural guess, because heat burns many things. But the needle is the same size and still made of steel.

flow.do: Talk about what happened.
flow.say: Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. Only the direction of the tiny magnets changed, twice.
flow.kid: Heat shook the tiny magnets out of line. Stroking lined them up again. Nothing was added. Nothing was taken away.
flow.think: The Earth's core is far hotter than 770 degrees. So how can the Earth be a magnet?

flow.do: 1. Choose a spot for the compass, far from iron, the fridge and phones. 2. Float the needle and let it settle. 3. Stick a paper label marked N on the table where the needle's north end points. 4. Write the first diary entry.
flow.say: Let's set up a compass station. The observatory in Alibag has measured the Earth's magnetic field like this for over a hundred years.
flow.kid: Pick a spot far from iron. Float your needle. Put a label N where it points. Write today's date and what you see.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Compass Diary, a 3-day project. You set up a compass and check it every day, like a real magnetic observatory.

flow.do: On day 2, check the compass twice and write what you see.

flow.wait: Come back tomorrow, and again the day after.
flow.parent: A steel needle usually stays magnetised for days or weeks, though it may get a little weaker. If it stops working, stroke it again and note that in the diary.

flow.kid: Draw your home from above. Use your compass to write N, E, S and W. Which way does your front door face?

check.q: You face north. Which way is east?
options: To your right
To your left
Behind you
check.why: Face north, and east is on your right, west is on your left, and south is behind you. Picking 'left' is a very common mix-up. A trick: the Sun rises in the east, so in the morning, face the Sun and north is on your left.

challenges.title: The Steady Compass
challenges.problem: A floating needle compass works well on a table, but it sloshes about on a moving bus, a boat or in your hand. Design a compass that still points north while you walk around with it.
constraints: You may use only things from home.
Your compass must work while you walk slowly across the room holding it.
Test it with a phone compass, held at least half a metre away.
materials: a pin or pushpin and a cork or eraser
cardboard, tape and a small paper cup
general: Hang the needle on a thread inside a clear bottle, so the wind can't move it.
Balance the needle on the point of a pin stuck upright in an eraser. This is a dry compass, like the ones on ships.
Use a small closed jar filled almost to the top with water, so the water can't slosh.
creative: Glue the needle under a paper arrow and balance the arrow on a pin, so it is easier to read.
Sailors in the Arabian Sea floated iron fish in bowls. Later, ship compasses hung in rings that tilt, so they stay level when the ship rolls. Can you make a swinging holder?
Float the needle on a slice of cork in a small closed jar of cooking oil. Oil is thicker than water, so the needle swings less.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own steady compass. Draw it, build it, and walk across the room with it. Does it still point north?

flow.do: 1. Float the needle compass in a bowl. 2. Pick the bowl up and walk slowly across the room. 3. Watch what the needle does.
flow.say: Let's see the problem first. What happens to our compass when we walk with it?
flow.kid: Pick up your floating compass. Walk across the room slowly. What does the needle do?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Steady Compass challenge. First you see why a floating compass is hard to use while moving.

flow.do: Before building, draw three ideas together.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. Let's think of three ways to keep the needle steady.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three ideas for a compass that won't slosh.

flow.do: 1. Build the best idea. 2. Walk across the room with it. 3. Check with a phone compass held away from it. 4. Improve it and test again.
flow.say: Build it and test it. Is it still pointing north while you walk?
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Walk with it. Check with a phone. Still pointing north? Make it better and try again.
flow.parent: The thread-in-a-bottle and pin-balance ideas usually work best. For the pin balance, push a pin upright through an eraser, and rest the needle's middle on its tip. A tiny dent of folded paper under the needle helps it balance. Keep phones and keys away, or the needle will turn to them.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together, then invent one more.
flow.say: Here's what compass makers usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you beat them?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and some creative ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Turtles and robins carry their compass inside them. It never sloshes. How might a body do that?

challenges.title: Iron-Proof: how far from iron must a compass be?
challenges.problem: In the story, a big iron pot made the ship's compass point the wrong way. Find out how close iron things at home must be before they turn your compass needle. Then choose the best spot in your home for a compass station.
constraints: Use a measuring tape or a string marked every 10 cm.
Test at least 3 iron things, like a steel almirah, a gas cylinder, an iron dosa tawa or a fridge.
Move the compass, not the heavy iron thing.
materials: a compass, or the needle on a thread
a measuring tape, or a string marked every 10 cm
general: Start right next to the iron thing. Move the compass back 10 cm at a time, until it points the same way as it does in the middle of the room.
Write down that distance for each thing.
creative: Draw a map of your home and colour a 'danger zone' around each iron thing. Where is the safe spot?
Test whether a closed laptop, a phone or a speaker turns the compass needle too. They have magnets inside.
Test the floor and walls. Many buildings have steel rods inside the concrete.
challenges.your_turn: Now find the safest spot in your home for a compass station, and explain why you chose it.

flow.do: 1. In the middle of the room, far from everything, see where the compass points. 2. Mark that direction on paper.
flow.say: First, where does the compass point when nothing nearby is turning it?
flow.kid: Stand in the middle of the room. Where does the compass point? Mark it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Iron-Proof. You measure how far a compass must be from iron things before they stop turning its needle.

flow.do: 1. Hold the compass right next to an iron thing. 2. Move back 10 cm at a time. 3. Stop when it points the normal way again. 4. Write down the distance. 5. Do this for 3 things.
flow.say: Move back 10 centimetres at a time. When does the needle go back to pointing the normal way?
flow.kid: Start next to the iron thing. Step back 10 cm at a time. When does the needle point the normal way again? Write the distance.
flow.parent: Big iron things turn a compass needle from further away. A steel almirah or a fridge can turn it from 50 cm to a metre away. A small iron dosa tawa, perhaps from 20 to 30 cm. Your numbers will differ.

flow.do: Draw a map with danger zones, and choose a safe spot.
flow.say: Where in our home is the safest spot for a compass?
flow.kid: Draw your home. Colour a danger zone around each iron thing. Where is the safe spot?

check.q: A steel almirah turns the compass needle from up to 80 cm away. An iron dosa tawa turns it from up to 25 cm away. Why the difference?
options: The almirah has much more iron, so its effect on the needle reaches further
The tawa is not really iron
Almirahs are made of a special magnet metal
check.why: More iron has a bigger effect on the compass needle, so the needle is turned from further away. Picking 'the tawa is not really iron' is a fair check. Test it with a magnet. If the magnet sticks, the tawa has iron in it. Picking 'special magnet metal' is a fair guess too, but almirahs are made of ordinary steel.

quiz.p: Rani's brass diya and her iron kadai are both made of metal. A magnet attracts the kadai but not the diya. Why?
opts: Brass has no iron, nickel or cobalt in it
quiz.why: A magnet attracts only metals with iron, nickel or cobalt in them. Brass is made of copper and zinc, so a magnet does not attract it. Picking 'too heavy' or 'too shiny' means thinking about how a thing looks, not what it is made of.

quiz.p: Some steel pins fell into a box of brass buttons. What is the quickest way to get the pins out?
opts: Hold a magnet over the box
Shine a torch into the box
quiz.why: The magnet attracts the steel pins but not the brass buttons, so the pins jump out and the buttons stay. Scrap dealers sort metals in the same way.

quiz.p: To make a needle into a magnet, how should you stroke it?
opts: Always in the same direction, lifting the magnet away each time
quiz.why: Each stroke in the same direction turns more of the needle's tiny magnets to point the same way. Stroking back and forth turns them back again. Picking 'just once, very hard' usually means thinking that force matters more than repeating the stroke.

quiz.p: A floating magnetised needle always turns to point north and south. Why?
opts: The Earth's magnetic field turns it
quiz.why: The needle is a magnet, and the Earth's magnetic field turns it to line up north and south. Picking the Pole Star comes from an old idea. Stars have no effect on compasses, and a compass works in a closed room.

quiz.p: Meera does the paper clip chain test. Her magnet holds 5 clips on the first try. Why should she test it two more times?
opts: The magnet gets stronger each time
One try can be a fluke, for example if a clip is bent or the chain is knocked
quiz.why: One result can be wrong by bad luck. If three tries give about the same number, she can trust it. If one try is very different, she knows to look for what went wrong. Picking 'gets stronger each time' means thinking testing changes the magnet. It does not.

quiz.p: In a fair test of which magnet is strongest, what should stay the same?
opts: The kind and size of paper clips
The number of clips each magnet holds
Nothing needs to stay the same
quiz.why: Everything except the magnet should stay the same, including the clips. If one magnet got smaller clips, it could hold more, and the test would not be fair. The number of clips is what we measure, so it changes.

quiz.p: Every electron is a tiny magnet. Why aren't you magnetic?
opts: Your electrons are in pairs pointing opposite ways, so they cancel
Your body has no iron in it
quiz.why: In most atoms, electrons are in pairs, and the two in each pair point their tiny magnets opposite ways. So they cancel out. Picking 'too small' sounds sensible, but iron's electrons are just as small. The difference is whether they cancel. Your body does have a little iron, in your blood, but those iron atoms are spread out, not lined up in domains.

opts: The two ends of a magnet
Small regions inside iron where the atoms' tiny magnets point the same way
The lines of the Earth's magnetic field
quiz.why: Domains are small regions inside iron, where billions of atoms point their tiny magnets the same way. In a plain nail they point different ways. In a magnet they mostly line up. Picking 'the two ends' mixes domains up with poles.

quiz.p: A magnetised needle is heated until it glows red. When it cools, it no longer picks up a pin. Why?
opts: The heat burned the iron away
The heat shook its tiny magnets out of line
Hot things are never magnetic, even after they cool
quiz.why: Heat is atoms jiggling. At about 770 degrees Celsius, iron's tiny magnets jiggle out of line, and they stay jumbled after it cools. Stroking it again can line them up again. Picking 'burned away' is natural, but the needle is still there, still steel.

opts: A natural magnet made of the mineral magnetite
A heavy iron weight on a ship
A magnet made in a factory
quiz.why: A lodestone is a piece of magnetite, a black mineral with iron in it, that is a magnet straight from the ground. People in Greece, China and India found them long ago.

quiz.p: In the old Indian surgery book, the Sushruta Samhita, what is a magnet used for?
opts: Drawing a smooth iron arrowhead out of a wound
quiz.why: The Sushruta Samhita describes using a magnet, called ayaskanta, to draw out iron arrowheads without barbs. A magnet attracts iron, but not skin. Picking 'finding north' mixes this up with the compass, which came into use later.

quiz.p: What makes the Earth a magnet?
opts: A giant bar magnet buried at the North Pole
Liquid iron moving in the Earth's outer core
The Moon pulling on the Earth
quiz.why: Liquid iron churns slowly in the outer core, which starts about 2,900 kilometres down. Electric currents flow in the moving iron, and electric currents make a magnetic field. Picking 'a giant bar magnet' is a common picture, but the core is far too hot for a solid magnet. Above about 770 degrees Celsius, iron cannot stay magnetised.

quiz.p: The Earth's magnetic field has flipped many times. After a flip, a compass would point south.
quiz.why: True. Old lava rocks are magnetised in both directions. The last flip was about 780,000 years ago. Motonori Matuyama showed this in 1929, from rocks in Japan, Korea and China.

quiz.p: Which of these living things has been shown to use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way?
quiz.why: Experiments by Kenneth and Catherine Lohmann show that young loggerhead turtles change direction when the magnetic field around them is changed. Robins and some bacteria use the field too. Picking 'only compasses can' is wrong, because animals sensed the Earth's magnetic field long before people made compasses.

quiz.p: Do scientists know exactly how birds sense the Earth's magnetic field?
opts: No. The leading idea is a protein in their eyes, but it is still being tested
Birds don't sense it at all
Yes, they have a tiny compass needle in their beaks
quiz.why: The leading idea is cryptochrome, a protein in birds' eyes that responds to magnetic fields. It is not yet fully proven. The beak idea was tested in 2012, and the iron cells there turned out to be immune cells that clean up the body, not magnetic sensors.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3 in Madurai, empties her pencil box and her mother's sewing tin onto the table. Sort each thing: will a magnet attract it?
items.a: see items
items.why: The pin, nail, clip and needle are attracted, because they are iron or steel, and steel is mostly iron. Brass, aluminium and copper are metals too, but they have no iron, nickel or cobalt in them. Rubber is not a metal at all. A strong answer sorts by what the thing is made of, not by whether it is shiny or hard.

items.p: Meenakshi says, 'Every metal sticks to a magnet.' Is she right?
items.why: False. Copper, brass, aluminium, gold and silver are all metals, and a magnet does not attract any of them. A magnet attracts iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt. A strong answer names one metal that does not stick, such as a brass key.

items.p: Lakshmi puts a steel pin on the table and lays a page of her notebook over it. She slides a magnet around on top of the page. What will the pin do?
opts: Follow the magnet around under the page
Stay still, because the paper blocks the magnet
Stick to the paper and stay there
items.why: The magnet's force acts through paper, cloth, wood and even your hand. So the pin follows the magnet under the page. Many people guess the paper blocks it. Try it and see.

items.p: A magnet can move a pin without touching it. Explain how. Use the words 'magnetic field' in your answer.
items.a: Every magnet has a magnetic field around it. This is the space where its force acts. When the pin is inside the magnetic field, the magnet attracts it, even across a gap.
items.why: A strong answer says that the force acts across the space around the magnet, the magnetic field, so nothing has to touch.

items.p: Draw a bar magnet that has been rolled in a heap of paper clips. Show where the clips cling. Label the north pole and the south pole.
items.a: Bunches of clips at the two ends, labelled north and south, and few or none in the middle.
items.why: A magnet's force is strongest at its two ends, the poles. A strong drawing shows that clearly, with the middle almost bare.
items.art: A blank outline of a bar magnet.

items.p: Anjali slides two ring magnets onto a pencil. They snap together. She takes the top one off, turns it over and slides it back on. What happens now?
opts: The top magnet floats above the bottom one
items.why: Turning the top magnet over puts the same kind of pole face to face, for example north facing north. Poles that are the same repel each other, so the top magnet floats. A strong answer says which poles now face each other.

items.p: When two magnets push each other away, we say they ____ each other.
items.why: Repel means push away. Two north poles, or two south poles, repel each other. A north pole and a south pole attract each other.

items.p: Revathi strokes a sewing needle 50 times with a magnet, always the same way. Now the needle picks up a pin. What changed inside the needle?
opts: Some iron moved from the magnet into the needle
The tiny magnets inside the needle now point the same way
items.why: Nothing passes from the magnet into the needle. The stroking turns the needle's own tiny magnets to point the same way, so their forces add up. A strong answer uses the words 'tiny magnets' and 'line up'.

items.p: A needle compass still points north and south inside a closed room with no windows.
items.why: True. The compass is turned by the Earth's magnetic field, which passes through walls. It does not need the Sun or the stars. Many people guess that a compass needs to 'see' the sky.

items.p: Arjun floats his needle compass in a steel bowl. The needle keeps swinging to the side of the bowl instead of pointing north. What is the best fix?
opts: Use a plastic or glass bowl instead
items.why: Some steel bowls are magnetic, so the bowl attracts the needle to its edge. A plastic or glass bowl is not magnetic, so only the Earth's magnetic field turns the needle. A strong answer says what was pulling the needle the wrong way.

items.p: A magnet attracts three of these metals. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Iron, nickel and cobalt are the three magnetic metals. Aluminium is a metal too, but a magnet does not attract it. That is why a magnet cannot pick up a cold drink can made of aluminium.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: an end of a magnet, where its force is strongest
the space around a magnet where its force acts
a magnet that can turn freely and points north and south
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could also give an example of each.

items.p: Farhan wants to find out which of his two magnets is stronger, using a paper clip chain. Which of these would make his test unfair?
opts: Using the same kind of clips for both magnets
Using big clips for one magnet and small clips for the other
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes: the magnet. Small clips are lighter, so a magnet could hold more of them. Then we could not tell if the magnet or the clips made the difference.

items.p: Two sisters in Chennai have a big flat fridge magnet and a tiny round magnet. They argue about which one is stronger.

views.says: The big one must be stronger. It is ten times bigger than the tiny one.
The tiny one is stronger. It is much harder to pull off the fridge door.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Use what you found in the paper clip chain test. Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence, such as the number of clips each magnet held. It sees that size is not the whole story: a tiny magnet made of a strong material can beat a big flexible one. It also gives the other sister her due. Kavya is right that, of two magnets made the same way, the bigger one is usually stronger. Divya is right that how hard it is to pull off is a real clue, but counting clips is fairer than feeling.
items.why: There is no single right answer without a test. Strength depends on what the magnet is made of and how well its tiny magnets line up, as well as its size.

items.p: Many people think a magnet attracts anything shiny. Plan a quick test at home to check this. Say which things you would test.
items.a: I would test shiny things that are not iron, such as aluminium foil, a brass diya and a steel tumbler, and dull things that are iron, such as an old rusty nail. If the shiny foil does not stick but the dull nail does, the idea is wrong.
items.why: A strong plan tests both shiny things that are not iron and dull things that are, so it can really show whether shininess matters.

items.p: Put the steps for making a needle compass in order.
items: Float the needle on a bit of paper in a bowl of water
Stroke the needle with a magnet 50 times, always one way
Check that the needle picks up a pin
Wait for it to stop turning, and check which way is north
a: Stroke the needle with a magnet 50 times, always one way
Check that the needle picks up a pin
Float the needle on a bit of paper in a bowl of water
Wait for it to stop turning, and check which way is north
items.why: First make the magnet, then check that it worked, then float it so it can turn freely, then read it.

items.p: Every electron is a tiny magnet, and copper has plenty of electrons. So why does a magnet not attract copper?
opts: In copper, the electrons' tiny magnets cancel each other out
items.why: In copper, the electrons' tiny magnets cancel out. Most of copper's electrons are in pairs that point opposite ways. Copper's few spare electrons never line up together. In iron, many spare electrons line up with their neighbours, so their tiny magnets add up. 'No electrons' is wrong, because every atom has electrons.

items.p: A plain steel nail is full of tiny magnets, but on its own it cannot pick up a pin. Explain why. Then explain why the same nail can pick up a pin while a magnet is touching it.
items.a: In a plain nail, the tiny magnets are in patches called domains, and the domains point different ways, so their forces cancel. When a magnet touches the nail, many of the domains turn to line up with the magnet's field. Now their forces add up, and the nail is a magnet for as long as the magnet stays.
items.why: A strong answer explains both halves: jumbled domains cancel, lined-up domains add up. It may mention the paper clip chain, where each clip becomes a magnet in the same way.

items.p: When you turn a needle into a magnet by stroking it, some of the magnet's magnetism moves into the needle, so the magnet gets weaker.
items.why: False. Nothing passes from the magnet to the needle. The stroking only lines up the needle's own tiny magnets. One magnet can magnetise hundreds of needles and stay just as strong.

items.p: In the heating test, a magnetised needle was heated until it glowed red. After it cooled, it no longer picked up a pin. Hema, aged 10, says, 'It can never be a magnet again.' Is she right? Say what you would do to find out.
items.a: I think she is wrong. The heat shook the tiny magnets out of line, but the needle is still steel. I would stroke it 50 times with a magnet, always the same way, and then see if it picks up a pin again.
items.why: A strong answer explains what the heat did, and gives a test that could prove Hema right or wrong. In the activity, the needle becomes a magnet again after stroking.

items.p: Sangeetha holds a magnet at different distances from a pin. Put these in order, from where the magnet's force on the pin is weakest to where it is strongest.
items.why: A magnet's force gets weaker very quickly as you move it away. That is why the pin only jumps up when the magnet is close.

items.p: Lakshmi does the paper clip chain test three times with each magnet. Fridge magnet: 1, 1, 2. Ceramic magnet: 4, 5, 4. Bar magnet: 6, 2, 6. Which result looks odd, and what should she do?
opts: The fridge magnet's 2. She should ignore the fridge magnet
The ceramic magnet's 5. She should start again
The bar magnet's 2. She should check the clips and try that magnet again
items.why: The bar magnet held 6 clips twice, so 2 is very different. Maybe a clip was bent or the chain was knocked. Testing again shows whether 2 was a fluke. This is why we test each magnet three times.

items.p: Priya holds a compass next to a steel almirah, and the needle swings towards it. Why?
opts: The almirah's iron attracts the needle, which is a magnet
The almirah has its own north pole for the Earth
items.why: A compass needle is a magnet, and a magnet and iron attract each other. The iron in the almirah turns the needle towards it, just as the iron pot did in the story 'The Iron Fish'. Move the compass far away and it points north again.

items.p: The temperature at which a magnet stops being a magnet is called the ____ point.
items.why: For iron, the Curie point is about 770 degrees Celsius. It is named after Pierre Curie, who measured it in 1895.

items.p: In the 'Gilbert's Little Earth' activity, a hanging needle pointed a different way at each place around a magnet. A compass on the Earth also points along curved lines from pole to pole. What does this suggest?
opts: The Earth acts like a giant magnet
The middle of the Earth is a huge lodestone
items.why: The needle behaved around the magnet the way compasses behave on the Earth. So William Gilbert said in 1600 that the Earth is a magnet. But it is not a lodestone inside. The core is far too hot for a solid magnet, so the field is made by moving liquid iron instead.

items.p: A compass needle points exactly at the North Pole.
items.why: False. It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, which points roughly towards the magnetic north pole. That is a different place from the North Pole, and it moves every year. Shen Kuo, a Chinese scientist, noticed the difference in 1088.

items.p: In the story 'The Iron Fish', Amina, a ten-year-old girl on a sailing ship, rubbed the iron fish with the black stone 'from tail to nose, never back and forth'. Explain why, using the words 'tiny magnets'.
items.a: Each stroke in one direction turns more of the tiny magnets inside the iron to point the same way. Rubbing back and forth would turn some of them back again, so they would stay jumbled.
items.why: A strong answer says that strokes in one direction line the tiny magnets up, and back-and-forth undoes the work.

items.p: In the black sand experiment, which of your samples gave the most black grains? Give a reason why that sample might have more.
items.a: For example: the sand from the building site gave the most. Building sand comes from rivers that wash it out of rocks, and some rocks have lots of magnetite. The pot plant soil gave almost none, because it is mostly old leaves and compost.
items.why: A strong answer uses the child's own result, and gives a reason about where that sand or soil came from and what it was made of.

items.p: Rukmini, a grandmother in Mysuru, wears a magnet bracelet for her sore knee. Her family talks about it.

views.says: My knee hurts less since I started wearing it. I can feel it working.
Careful tests found that people feel just as much better with fake magnets as with real ones. So the magnet is not doing it.
If Paati feels better and the bracelet does no harm, that matters. But it must not stop her from getting her knee checked.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer back from another person's side.
items.a: A strong answer uses the evidence: in tests where people did not know if their bracelet was real or fake, both groups felt about the same, so the magnet itself is not easing the pain. It also takes Paati seriously, because the pain she feels is real and feeling better is real too. And it sees the doctor's point about not skipping real treatment.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. The science says magnet bracelets do not work by magnetism. But expecting to feel better can really make people feel better, and that is not nothing.

items.p: Draw two squares of iron as if you were looking from very, very close. In the first square, draw the tiny magnets as arrows for a plain nail. In the second, draw them for a magnet.
items.a: Plain nail: patches of arrows, each patch pointing a different way. Magnet: nearly all the arrows pointing the same way.
items.why: This shows domains: jumbled in a plain nail, lined up in a magnet. A strong drawing shows patches, not single random arrows.
items.art: Two empty squares side by side.

items.p: Scientists kept European robins, a kind of small bird, in a cage and changed the magnetic field around them with coils of wire. The robins then tried to fly in a different direction. Why is this good evidence that robins sense the magnetic field?
opts: The test was done at night
Only the magnetic field was changed, and the robins changed too
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here the light, food and cage stayed the same and only the magnetic field changed. So the change in the robins' direction must come from the field. Wolfgang and Roswitha Wiltschko did tests like this from 1972.

items.p: Match each thing that happens to its cause.
pairs: stroking it one way lines up its tiny magnets
A magnet stops being a magnet
heating it red-hot shakes its tiny magnets out of line
A paper clip holds up another clip
a magnet nearby turns the first clip into a magnet for a while
A compass points the wrong way
a piece of iron is close to it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All four come from one idea: magnetism depends on whether the tiny magnets inside the iron line up.

items.p: The Earth's core is far hotter than 770 degrees Celsius, the temperature at which iron stops being a magnet. So how can the Earth be a magnet?
items.a: The Earth is not a magnet because of lined-up domains. Liquid iron moves slowly in the outer core. Electric currents flow in the moving iron, and electric currents make a magnetic field. That works at any temperature.
items.why: A strong answer joins two ideas from the unit: heat stops domains staying lined up, but moving electric charge makes a magnetic field however hot it is.

items.p: Three people are talking about who first used a magnet to find the way.

views.says: Chinese books from 1044 and 1088 describe magnet compasses. That is the oldest dated evidence, so China came first.

views.who: Kalyani, a history teacher in Kochi
views.says: Some books say Indian sailors used an iron fish compass called a matsya yantra. Sailors don't always write things down, so they may have used it earlier than any book says.

views.who: Rashida, who studies old sea routes
views.says: By 1232, a writer at the Delhi court described sailors floating an iron fish rubbed with a lodestone. Maybe people in many places found the idea, each on their own.

items.ask: Which view do you find most convincing? Give your reason. Then say what evidence would make you change your mind.
items.a: A strong answer asks for dated evidence: a book, a map or an object that can be dated. It sees that Mei has the oldest dated texts, that Kalyani's point about unwritten knowledge is fair but hard to prove, and that Rashida's idea fits the evidence too. It names one find, such as an old dated Indian text, that would change its mind.
items.why: Historians still argue about this. The oldest dated descriptions we have are Chinese. Whether others found it earlier, or on their own, is not settled.

items.p: A scientist sees that tiny bacteria in a dish always swim towards the north. She turns a magnet around the dish, and the bacteria turn too. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The bacteria are swimming towards the light
The bacteria can see the Pole Star
The bacteria respond to magnetic fields
items.why: Changing only the magnetic field changed which way the bacteria swam. That is good evidence that they respond to magnetic fields. 'Towards the light' is a fair idea, but the light did not change. These magnetic bacteria build chains of magnetite crystals inside their bodies.

items.p: In satellite pictures, cows in fields seemed to stand facing north and south. A later study found no pattern. If you were a scientist, what would you do next?
items.a: I would watch cows myself, in many places, and write down which way each one faces. I would also write down the wind and where the Sun is, because those could change which way cows stand.
items.why: A strong answer repeats the study and thinks about other causes that could explain the pattern.

items.p: Imagine the Earth's magnetic field flipped. What would your needle compass do? Do you think sea turtles would still find their way? Explain.
items.a: My needle compass would point the opposite way: its north end would point south. A flip takes thousands of years, and turtles have lived through many flips, so I think they would slowly adjust. But nobody knows for sure how their magnetic sense would cope.
items.why: A strong answer gets the compass right, uses the fact that flips are slow and have happened many times, and is honest that the turtle part is not known. The last flip was about 780,000 years ago.

items.p: Andre Geim, a scientist, made a live frog float inside a giant magnet. The frog has hardly any iron in their body. Explain how this can be.
items.a: Every material responds to a magnet a little. Water, which makes up most of a frog, is very slightly repelled by a magnet. In a giant magnet, this tiny push is strong enough to hold the frog up.
items.why: A strong answer sees that 'not magnetic' really means 'very, very weakly magnetic'. The frog was unharmed.

items.p: Mars has almost no magnetic field around the whole planet. Why do many scientists think Mars lost much of its air?
opts: Without a magnetic field to steer it away, the Sun's solar wind stripped the air away
The air all froze into ice caps
Mars is too far from the Sun to have air
items.why: The Earth's magnetic field steers the solar wind, the Sun's stream of tiny charged particles, around our planet. Mars lost its field long ago, so the solar wind slowly stripped its air. Some air froze into the ice caps, but not most of it.

items.p: Sangeetha snaps a bar magnet in half. What does she get?
opts: One piece that is only a north pole and one that is only a south pole
Two smaller magnets, each with a north pole and a south pole
Two pieces that are not magnets at all
One magnet and one piece that is not a magnet
items.why: Most people guess that one half would be only a north pole and the other only a south pole. But the tiny magnets inside are still lined up in each half, so each half is a whole magnet with two poles. You can test this with a cheap broken fridge magnet.

items.p: In 1904, the magnetic observatory in Colaba, Bombay, moved to Alibag, a quiet town across the bay. Electric trams were coming to Bombay. Why did the scientists move?
opts: The trams' electric currents would make magnetic fields and spoil the measurements
items.why: Electric currents make magnetic fields. The observatory measured the Earth's magnetic field very carefully, and the trams' currents would have added their own fields to the readings.

items.p: Design an experiment to test whether ants can sense a magnet. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would watch.
items.a: I would put a little sugar in the middle of a round plate and let ants come to it. Then I would put a strong magnet under one side of the plate, and later under the other side. I would keep the light, the sugar and the plate the same. I would count how many ants walk towards the magnet's side each time.
items.why: A strong design changes only the magnet, keeps everything else the same, counts what happens, and tests more than once.

items.p: The Earth's magnetic north pole moves about 40 kilometres a year. How far might it move in 10 years?
items.why: 40 kilometres each year, for 10 years, is 40 times 10, which is 400 kilometres. That is why maps that show compass directions are updated every few years.

items.p: Arjun says, 'A magnet attracts iron because iron is heavy and magnets are strong.' What is wrong with his idea? Describe a test that would show it.
items.a: Weight is not what matters. A light steel pin is attracted, but a heavy brass diya is not. I would hold a magnet near a tiny pin and a heavy brass vessel. The pin jumps to the magnet and the brass does not move.
items.why: A strong answer says that what the thing is made of matters, not how heavy it is, and gives a test with a light iron thing and a heavy thing that is not iron.

items.p: Draw the Earth cut in half. Label the crust, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core. Draw curved magnetic field lines around the outside.
items.a: A thin crust, a thick rocky middle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, with curved field lines looping from one pole round to the other.
items.why: This shows where the Earth's magnetic field is made, in the moving liquid outer core, and its shape. Inge Lehmann, a Danish scientist, showed in 1936 that the inner core is solid.
items.art: An empty circle for the Earth.

items.p: Nobody has ever found a magnet with only one pole.
items.why: True. Physicists have searched for single-pole magnets, called monopoles, for nearly a hundred years, and have never found one. Every magnet ever found has two poles.

items.p: Some magnets are made by tiny magnets lined up inside a solid. Others are made by electric charge moving. Sort these.
items: a wire with electricity flowing in it
items.a: see items
items.why: These are the two ways to make a magnetic field. The Earth's field comes from moving liquid iron, which carries electric currents. A strong answer can explain why the Earth cannot be the first kind: its core is too hot.

items.p: Put these in order, to show how the Earth's magnetic field turns your compass.
items: Electric currents flow in the moving iron
Your compass needle lines up with the field
Liquid iron moves slowly in the outer core
The currents make a magnetic field around the whole Earth
a: Liquid iron moves slowly in the outer core
Electric currents flow in the moving iron
The currents make a magnetic field around the whole Earth
Your compass needle lines up with the field
items.why: Each step causes the next. The field starts about 2,900 kilometres under your feet and reaches the needle in your bowl.

applications: Compasses for sailors, hikers, pilots and soldiers.
Fridge doors and cupboard catches stay shut with magnets.
Scrap yards and recycling plants lift iron and steel out of mixed waste with giant magnets.
Every electric fan, mixer, washing machine and car motor has magnets inside.
Most power stations spin magnets near coils of wire to make electricity.
Speakers, earphones and phone vibrators use magnets to make sound and buzzing.
Hospitals use MRI scanners, with huge magnets, to see inside the body without cutting.
Maglev trains, like the one in Shanghai, float above the track, held up by magnetic force.
Hard disks and the magnetic strips on old bank cards store information as tiny lined-up magnets.
Small, very strong neodymium magnets, invented in the 1980s, are used in wind turbines and electric cars.
Doctors once used magnets to draw iron splinters out of eyes and wounds, as the Sushruta Samhita describes.
Geologists use magnetometers, instruments that measure magnetic fields, to find iron ore and to read the history of the Earth's magnetic field in old rocks.
Scientists use the magnetic bacteria's tiny crystals to study how living things build minerals.
Magnetic observatories, like the one at Alibag, help warn about solar storms that can disturb power lines and satellites.

open_questions.q: What is an electron's spin, really?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure it very exactly and use it every day, but cannot say what it is underneath. Some think it needs no further explanation.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do birds sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: The leading idea is cryptochrome, a protein in their eyes that works through electron spins. It has been shown in the lab but not yet fully proven in living birds.

open_questions.q: Can people sense the Earth's magnetic field, even without knowing it?
open_questions.why_open: One 2019 study found brainwave changes in some people. It has not yet been repeated by other teams.

open_questions.q: When will the Earth's magnetic field flip next?
open_questions.why_open: Flips don't come on a schedule. The field has weakened a little over the last 200 years, but that may or may not mean a flip is coming. Nobody can predict it yet.

open_questions.q: Why does the magnetic north pole move so fast, and why did it speed up and then slow down?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how the liquid iron moves deep in the core, which nobody can see directly. Scientists use computer models and argue about them.

open_questions.q: Do magnetic monopoles, magnets with only one pole, exist anywhere?
open_questions.why_open: Some theories say they should have been made just after the universe began. Physicists have searched for nearly a hundred years and found none.

open_questions.q: How exactly did lodestones become magnets?
open_questions.why_open: Lightning explains some, but maybe not all. Scientists are still studying which kinds of magnetite hold their magnet best.

open_questions.q: How does the hot liquid core keep making a magnetic field for billions of years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists call the moving iron in the core the geodynamo. It is so complicated that computers can only copy it roughly. How the Earth's magnetic field first started, and how it has lasted, are still argued about.

maths.problem: In the paper clip chain test, the neodymium magnet held 12 clips. The ceramic magnet held 4 clips. How many times as many clips did the neodymium magnet hold?
maths.explain: The neodymium magnet held 12 clips and the ceramic magnet held 4. 12 divided by 4 is 3. So it held 3 times as many. Check: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
maths.context: This is about the paper clip chain test. You hang paper clips in a chain from a magnet, one at a time, and count how many it can hold before one falls.

chart.title: Paper clips held in a chain

maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'this magnet is stronger'. Dividing one number by the other tells us how many times stronger.

maths.problem: To make a needle into a magnet, you stroke it in 5 rounds of 10 strokes. How many strokes is that altogether?
maths.explain: Each round is 10 strokes. There are 5 rounds. 5 groups of 10 is 50. You can count in tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
maths.context: This is about the floating needle compass. You stroke a needle with a magnet, always the same way, to turn it into a magnet.
maths.why_maths: Counting 50 strokes one by one is easy to lose. Counting in equal groups of 10 keeps your place.

maths.problem: The Chinese book Wujing Zongyao described an iron fish compass in 1044. William Gilbert said the Earth is a magnet in 1600. How many years apart are they?
maths.explain: Take the earlier year from the later year. 1600 take away 1044. 1600 take away 1000 is 600. 600 take away 44 is 556. So they are 556 years apart.
maths.context: This is about the magnet timeline on a string. You make cards for discoveries about magnets and hang them in order.
maths.why_maths: A timeline shows which came first. Subtracting the years tells us how long people used compasses before anyone knew why they worked.

maths.problem: Look at the map of your home. You stand at the front door facing north. You turn to face east, then turn again to face south. How many quarter turns did you make, and which way did you turn?
maths.answer: 2 quarter turns, both to the right. That is a half turn.
maths.explain: North to east is one quarter turn to the right. East to south is another quarter turn to the right. 1 + 1 = 2 quarter turns. Two quarter turns make a half turn, so now you face the opposite way from north.
maths.context: This is about My Compass Diary, where you use a compass to mark north, east, south and west on a map of your home.
maths.why_maths: A compass shows you north. To find east, south and west, you turn from north in quarter turns.

maths.problem: Look at the scale. It shows how far a compass was from a steel almirah when the almirah stopped turning its needle. Each big mark is 10 cm. Each small mark is 5 cm. What is the reading?
maths.explain: The pointer is past the 70 mark but before 80. It sits on the small mark halfway between them. Each small mark is 5 cm. 70 + 5 = 75. So the compass had to be 75 cm away.
maths.context: This is about the Iron-Proof challenge. You move a compass away from an iron thing, 10 cm at a time, until it points the normal way again.
maths.why_maths: A measuring tape only helps if you can read the marks between the numbers. That turns 'quite far' into an exact distance.

roots.context: We have learned how magnets attract iron, and about the tiny electron magnets inside iron. Now we ask what magnets tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A steel needle can be a magnet one minute and not the next. Stroke it with a magnet, and its tiny magnets line up. Heat it red-hot, and they fall out of line. So the same steel can be a magnet or not, depending only on which way its tiny magnets point.
deep_truth.habit: We sort objects into 'magnets' and 'not magnets', as if a magnet were made of a special material. But a needle becomes a magnet and stops being one while staying the same steel. What changes is the direction its tiny magnets point.
deep_truth.evidence: Stroke a needle and it picks up a pin. Heat it red-hot and it stops. Stroke it again and it picks up the pin again. Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. Only the direction of its tiny magnets changed.

three.who_am_i: Your body is full of electrons, and each one is a tiny magnet. In you, they are in pairs that cancel out.
three.what_is_life: Turtles, robins and tiny bacteria sense the Earth's magnetic field and use it to find their way.
three.what_is_this_world: The whole Earth is a magnet. Its magnetic field is made by moving liquid iron far beneath your feet.

roots.thread: Inside a plain nail, countless tiny magnets point in every direction. Their forces add up to zero, a perfect balance. Turn them to point the same way, and a magnetic force appears out of that zero. Nothing new was made. That one force then acts on many things: a pin, a ship's compass, a turtle's journey and the lights in the sky. This is a small picture of the One becoming the many: what is already there, arranged in a new way.

teachings.link: Tiny magnets that each point their own way cancel out. When they all point the same way, together they make a magnetic force that none of them has alone.

teachings.link: Every magnet has two poles, north and south, and nobody has ever found one without the other. In a plain nail, the forces of the tiny magnets balance out exactly.

science.text: Every electron is a tiny magnet. In most atoms the electrons pair up and cancel. In iron, their tiny magnets line up in domains.
Electricity, magnetism and light are one force, electromagnetism. Maxwell joined them in 1865.
What an electron's spin is, underneath, has no agreed answer.

other_view.view: Lining up is simply how electrons in iron behave. It is a beautiful fact, but it carries no message about agreement or oneness. Reading lessons into iron says more about us than about iron.

practice.title: Be the needle
practice.say: Let's stand up and close our eyes. Without peeking, point to where you think north is. Now open your eyes and check with the compass. Now let's all turn to face north together. Stand still and take six slow breaths. We are like the tiny magnets in a needle, all facing the same way. Each of us is still the same person. Only the direction we face has changed.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Point to where you think north is. Open your eyes and check the compass. Now face north. Breathe slowly six times. You are still you. Only your direction changed.

ask: When a needle becomes a magnet, nothing is added to it. Is the magnetised needle a new object, or the same needle?
In a plain nail, the tiny magnets cancel out to zero. Is their magnetic force gone, or only hidden?
A turtle finds their beach without a map. What do they sense that we do not notice?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. Changes made: bendy fridge magnets are often too weak to magnetise a needle and hold 0 or 1 clips, so the needle compass now asks for a bar, ceramic or neodymium magnet and says what to do if the pin won't lift. The floating needle uses a plastic, glass or clay bowl, because some steel bowls are magnetic, and the bowl sits a metre from the stove, fridge, almirah and phones. The needle often drifts to the bowl's edge, so the step says to nudge the paper back with a pencil. North is checked with a phone held half a metre away, or by facing the morning Sun. The black sand test wraps the magnet in a plastic bag, because magnetite stuck straight onto a strong magnet is very hard to clean, and it says which sands give most and what to try if nothing sticks. The heat activity needs a gas stove and a grown-up with tongs, and gives an alternative for homes with induction cooktops. The paper clip chain needs plain steel clips, all the same size. Parents should know: small neodymium magnets must be kept from children under 5, because two swallowed magnets can pinch the gut. Indian coins differ, and some are magnetic, which is a good surprise, not a mistake. Both games work for one child alone. Monsoon Voyage races the storm cloud, and Magnet Says uses 12 paper arrows. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, people knew that a compass points north, but not why. Some said the Pole Star attracted the needle. Others said there was a giant magnetic mountain far in the north. In 1581, Robert Norman, a compass maker in London, noticed something new. He balanced a magnetised needle so it could tilt up and down. It did not lie flat. Its north end dipped down towards the ground. Then William Gilbert, an English doctor, tested the idea that the Earth is a magnet. He carved a ball out of lodestone and called it a terrella, which means 'little Earth'. He moved a tiny needle over it. Near the middle of the ball, the needle lay flat. Near the poles of the ball, it tipped down, just as Norman's needle did in London. In 1600 Gilbert wrote a book, De Magnete, saying that the Earth itself is a giant magnet. That is why a compass points north. Gilbert thought the inside of the Earth was solid lodestone. That part was wrong. The core is far too hot to stay a magnet. Today we know the Earth's magnetic field is made by moving liquid iron.
how_we_found_out.who: Robert Norman, a London compass maker, and William Gilbert, an English doctor
how_we_found_out.when: 1581 (Norman's dipping needle) and 1600 (Gilbert's book De Magnete)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a compass was attracted by the Pole Star, or by a magnetic mountain in the far north. Gilbert's lodestone ball showed that the Earth itself is a magnet. Gilbert in turn thought the Earth's inside was solid lodestone. That was wrong too: the core is too hot, and the field comes from moving liquid iron.
